terms.gloss: entangle; make (a matter) hard to manage
evidence: Ter. And. 3.5.11: vidēn’ mē cōnsiliīs tuīs miserum impedītum esse? (Lewis & Short)
Ter. And. 3.5.13: rem impedītam, “an intricate affair” (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Literally to shackle the feet; hence to entangle a person or an affair so that it is hard to get free. Its commonest sense is plainly “hinder, prevent” (Lewis & Short), so for “complicate” name what is entangled: rem, sē, the plan.

evidence: Cic. Fin. 3.3: nec in Torquātī sermōne quicquam implicātum aut tortuōsum fuit (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The participle implicātus is the nearest classical word for “complicated”: intricate, involved. The verb more often means to involve someone in something (negōtiīs implicārī, Cic. Off. 2.40, Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: vidēn’ mē cōnsiliīs tuīs miserum impedītum esse?
phrases.english: don’t you see that your schemes have got poor me into a tangle?

phrases.latin: dum aliōs servat, sē impedīvit interim
phrases.english: while he was saving others, he got himself into a tangle

phrases.latin: nec in Torquātī sermōne quicquam implicātum aut tortuōsum fuit
phrases.english: and there was nothing complicated or tortuous in what Torquatus said

phrases.latin: Nōlī rem impedīre: satis est difficilis.
phrases.english: Don’t complicate it: it’s hard enough.

sources: Lewis & Short: impedio · Lewis & Short: implico
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, with its references, in the house spelling (macrons, consonantal j); they have not been checked against a modern edition.
